title: SICK TRADE IN AUSSIE ACCOUNTS
full_text:
Criminals are buying and selling thousands of Australian bank accounts on social media for as little as $200, creating a pipeline of “mule accounts” used to launder cash stolen from scam victims.
An investigation by The Daily Telegraph has uncovered a thriving underground market where Aussies are being recruited on Facebook to hand over bank accounts that can be used to funnel money from scam victims. Scammers have already stolen almost $100m from hardworking Australians so far this year, according to the Australian Competition and Consumer Commission (ACCC), despite fewer scams being reported now than at the same time last year.
Meanwhile, victims are now losing a mean $1540 – almost double the 2020 average. Alastair MacGibbon, former Adviser to the Prime Minister on Cybersecurity, said the practice of buying and selling bank accounts online was “absolutely outrageous” and should be blocked by social media platforms, calling on Meta to take responsibility.
“Those accounts being traded on platforms like Meta only have one use, and that is a criminal use,” he said.
The Courier-Mail identified and engaged multiple users openly advertising Australian bank accounts for sale and rent across social media and messaging platforms.
Accounts with small banks were offered as cheap as $200, while accounts with Westpac, St George, Suncorp and Bendigo Bank were listed at $600 or more.
In one exchange, a seller claiming to have access to accounts from St George and Up Bank said buyers would need “an Australian number, identification documents and a deposit”.
When asked whose name an Up Bank account was registered to, the seller replied: “My girlfriend’s.” Another seller offered Commonwealth Bank and Westpac accounts for “$300 each”. In a third conversation, a user seeking to purchase Australian accounts claimed they were needed “to receive $20,000”. When asked who would be sending the money, the user replied: “my boss”.
Mr MacGibbon said the sellers included international students or people leaving the country, whose accounts are then repurposed by criminals as “money mules” to move stolen funds through the financial system.
“Thousands” of accounts across all Australian financial institutions are caught up in it, he said.
“Criminals create chains of accounts because you need to take cash from a controlled account to an uncontrolled account and then out of the Australian system – whether that’s through international transfers, cash withdrawals or crypto,” Mr MacGibbon said.
Westpac Head of Fraud Prevention Ben Young said the bank was receiving reports in the “vicinity” of dozens of bank accounts being sold each week, describing Facebook groups as a marketplace where criminals and willing account holders could easily find each other.
“Facebook certainly has more than its fair share of these sorts of chat groups and forums, where people either offer to sell their accounts or people will … offer to buy the accounts, and so it just becomes a marketplace for selling bank accounts,” he said.
Mr Young said the issue first cropped up about three years ago and became serious enough for Westpac to raise concerns directly with Meta last year.
Mule accounts act as a buffer between scammers and their victim, he said, while banks are increasingly forced to act as the “last line of defence”.
“Rather than directing stolen money into an account linked to the criminal, scammers recruit or buy access to legitimate bank accounts and convince victims to transfer funds there instead,” he said.
“Once the money arrives, it is quickly moved on – often through multiple accounts or cryptocurrency – making it harder for banks and investigators to trace.” Mr MacGibbon said: “Ultimately, a bank account is an identity credential. “There is no legitimate reason – zero – to be able to sell or buy an Australian bank account. It’s tied to you as a person – it can only be used for crime.” A Meta spokesman said the company was investigating the pages “and will take action on them if they violate our policies”.
“Meta doesn’t want scams on our platforms, and we are continuing to invest in tools and technology to prevent them,” he said. “On Money Mule accounts flagged through the AFCX (Australian Financial Crimes Exchange) we acted against almost 2000 users, over 150 pages, over 50 groups, and several ad accounts.”
